title: UK PM Burnham Opens 'No10 North' in Manchester to Shift Power From London
excerpt: Britain's new prime minister launches a Manchester-based government hub and revives the National Economic Council as part of his devolution agenda.
body:
• British PM Andy Burnham has opened "No10 North" in Manchester, a new government base intended to shift economic decision-making away from London.
  • The office will host the revived National Economic Council, bringing together senior ministers and regional mayors to coordinate growth strategy.
  • Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has criticised the move, saying Burnham is "behaving like he's still the mayor of Manchester."
  • The initiative could reshape how NRIs and diaspora businesses engage with UK regional economies beyond London.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday opened a new government base in Manchester dubbed "No10 North," a move designed to decentralise economic decision-making from London and redistribute power to Britain's regions.

Burnham, who became prime minister on Monday after succeeding Keir Starmer, is moving quickly to put his stamp on government. The former Greater Manchester mayor has long argued that decades of London-centric policymaking have held back cities and regions across England.

A 'Situation Room' for Regional Growth

No10 North will initially operate from Heron House in central Manchester, a city-centre office building that also houses Britain's intelligence, cyber and security agency northern hub. Burnham described the new base as "the situation room for making Britain better — the place we use to get power out of Westminster, into the hands of people at a local level, so that they can turn things around."

"The days of Whitehall resisting devolution are over, for good."

— Andy Burnham, British Prime Minister

The prime minister is expected to work from the Manchester site each week, with other ministers also regularly using the office, according to the government.

Reviving the National Economic Council

Burnham will use No10 North to chair the first meeting of a revived National Economic Council, a cabinet-level body bringing together senior ministers and regional mayors to coordinate the government's economic growth strategy. The council was first established in London during the 2008 financial crisis by Gordon Brown to coordinate the government's response to the economic downturn, according to Reuters.

The new iteration shifts the council's focus from crisis management to long-term regional growth, with Burnham pledging to give regional mayors greater control over social housing, welfare, and post-16 education.

Opposition Pushback

The move has drawn criticism from opposition Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, who questioned whether Burnham's regional focus translates to effective national government. She said Burnham was "behaving like he's still the mayor of Manchester" and needed to address broader national challenges, according to Reuters.

The Institute for Government has noted that while rethinking the No10 operation is overdue, splitting it between London and Manchester carries complications. Parliament, ministers, and many civil servants are based in London, and the prime minister will need daily support from a London-based team.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora in the UK — a significant presence in cities like Birmingham, Leicester, and Manchester — the shift could open new economic corridors beyond London. Burnham's devolution agenda envisions regional mayors wielding greater influence over housing, transport, energy, and employment, areas where diaspora communities have substantial stakes.

Burnham has cast his premiership as a "circuit-breaker" from the politics of recent years, promising to reindustrialise the country and help young people into jobs. With an estimated 1.9 million people of Indian origin in the UK, many concentrated outside London, the devolution push may create new opportunities for community engagement with local government.
